name: Availability Heuristic
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: What Comes to Mind First: The Availability Heuristic in Crypto Risk Judgment
lesson.summary: The availability heuristic is the mental shortcut of judging how likely or common something is by how easily examples come to mind, a shortcut that badly distorts how people assess both the risks and the rewards of blockchain investing.
lesson.body:
The availability heuristic, described by Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman in a 1973 paper, is the mental shortcut of estimating the frequency or probability of an event by how easily examples of it come to mind, rather than by consulting actual data on how often it occurs. In one of their demonstrations, people judged that words starting with the letter k were more common in English than words with k as the third letter, because the first case is far easier to recall, even though the opposite is actually true. Ease of recall is being used as a stand in for actual frequency, and the two frequently diverge.

What makes an example easy to recall has little to do with how common it actually is. Recent events are easier to recall than older ones, vivid and emotionally charged events are easier to recall than mundane ones, and anything covered repeatedly in the news or social media becomes easier to recall regardless of its true statistical frequency. A single dramatic story, well told and widely shared, can outweigh a much larger body of unremarkable data simply because the dramatic story is what comes to mind.

Blockchain risk assessment is shaped heavily by this shortcut. Highly publicized exchange collapses and large scale fraud cases dominate media coverage precisely because they are dramatic, and that coverage makes such events easy to recall. As a result, people frequently overestimate how likely it is that any given crypto project or exchange is fraudulent, because the available examples in memory are the extreme, newsworthy failures rather than the much larger and less visible population of projects that were simply mediocre, underused, or quietly discontinued without ever making headlines. The heuristic distorts risk judgment in the direction of whatever failure mode happened to be most recently or most vividly reported, rather than toward the actual base rate of that failure mode across the full population of projects.

The same shortcut also inflates optimism in the other direction. Stories of extraordinary price gains are vivid, widely shared, and easy to recall, so people evaluating whether to buy a given token tend to overestimate the probability of a large gain, because the examples that come to mind most readily are the standout successes rather than the much larger number of unremarkable or negative outcomes. This works hand in hand with survivorship bias, discussed earlier, since the very examples that are easiest to recall are, by construction, the ones that survived and became prominent enough to be talked about.

Countering the availability heuristic in blockchain evaluation means deliberately seeking out base rate data, such as how many new token launches from a given period are still actively used a year later, rather than relying on whichever examples happen to be top of mind. It also helps to explicitly ask whether a given event is memorable because it is common or because it is dramatic, since those are very different properties, and treating recent, vivid news coverage as evidence about what is typical, rather than evidence about what is newsworthy, is one of the more reliable ways this particular shortcut leads evaluation astray.
